item.title: US Coast Guard finds debris from missing medical aircraft off Nantucket
item.description: The US Coast Guard said late on Saturday it found debris from a medical transport aircraft off the shore of Massachusetts' Nantucket island and was searching for six people who were on board.
item.dc:creator: Sheila Dang, Lisa Richwine
item.content:encoded: The US Coast Guard said late on Saturday it found debris from a medical transport aircraft off the shore of Massachusetts' Nantucket island and was searching for six people who were on board. The Federal Aviation Administration told the Coast Guard early on Saturday that it had lost contact with a Gulfstream jet traveling from Bermuda to Boston. Several hours later, the Coast Guard said in a statement that it "located a debris field that has been confirmed to be associated with the missing aircraft." Four Canadians were on the plane, Canadian Minister of Transport Steven MacKinnon said on X. "We are closely monitoring the situation and are working with the relevant authorities as search and rescue efforts continue," he wrote. The other two passengers were Bermudian nationals, the Coast Guard said. Searches will continue throughout the night near Nantucket, an island community south of mainland Massachusetts, they said. The aircraft, registered to Latitude Air Ambulance, departed Bermuda at 12:41 a.m. on Saturday (0301 GMT), according to data from flight tracking website FlightAware. The plane was flying at 24,000 feet (7,300 metres) for much of the flight before descending 13,000 feet in about two minutes shortly before flight controllers lost contact, data showed. Local TV station Boston 25 posted an audio clip from Boston Logan International Airport in which an air traffic controller can be heard asking the Gulfstream pilot, "You said you're coming in blind? Is that what you said?" The controller then asked whether the plane was declaring an emergency. No response was heard. Latitude is based in Ontario, Canada, and provides medical evacuation services. The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The Bermuda government is in contact with US authorities and the families of the passengers, Bermuda Premier David Burt wrote in a statement posted on Instagram. "We are praying that all six people will be found safe," he wrote.

item.title: Yemen's Houthis say they attacked Aramco facility in Riyadh with missiles, drones
item.description: Aramco did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said on Saturday they had targeted an Aramco facility in the Saudi capital Riyadh with ballistic missiles and drones, saying the attack was in retaliation for Saudi attacks on Yemen's Sanaa and other provinces. A large plume of smoke and fire was seen rising in the vicinity of an Aramco facility in Riyadh earlier on Saturday, a witness told Reuters. There was no immediate confirmation from Saudi authorities of an attack on an Aramco facility. Aramco did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The reported attack comes amid escalating hostilities between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, who have stepped up attacks on Saudi cities and energy infrastructure. The Houthis said last week they had attacked Saudi Aramco facilities in Yanbu with missiles and drones. Saudi Arabia said at the time that it had intercepted six ballistic missiles fired by the Houthis towards Taif and the Yanbu area, but did not report damage to Aramco facilities.

item.title: In crude Ohio rally speech, Trump says he may not help if Democrats win
item.description: "Just get out and vote," Trump said at a rally for Republican candidates. "If you do that, we're going to win, and we're going to win big, and we're going to shove it up their ass."
item.dc:creator: Bo Erickson, Nandita Bose
item.content:encoded: US President Donald Trump used an Ohio rally on Saturday to mix profane attacks on Democrats with promises of financial help if Republicans win the midterms and a warning that he would be less willing to work with the state if Democrats prevail. "Just get out and vote," Trump said at a rally for Republican candidates, including US Senator Jon Husted and Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy. "If you do that, we're going to win, and we're going to win big, and we're going to shove it up their ass." Multiple incumbent Republican senators across the country face tough political headwinds in the November 3 elections, with Trump's [USN:L6N45D0XN TEXT:"popularity falling"] in recent months as higher prices persist for gasoline and other staples amid the US-Israeli war with Iran. Both Husted and Ramaswamy are in competitive races against Democratic opponents. Former US Senator Sherrod Brown is running against Husted. Amy Acton is facing Ramaswamy. OHIO A KEY STATE IN MIDTERMS Polls have suggested that Democrats could gain ground in the midterms, which will decide control of the narrowly divided House of Representatives and Senate, but Trump said Republicans would do better than critics expect. "I think we're going to have a big surprise because they don't know what's happening," he told the crowd in Vandalia, Ohio. Ohio's is among eight US Senate races rated competitive. The state has turned into a campaign battlefield over [USN:L6N45916H TEXT:"data centers"] and culture war issues such as youth transgender surgeries. Trump repeatedly attacked Democrats during his speech, at one point calling them "dumb son of a bitches," while arguing that maintaining Republican control would give Ohio officials a direct line to his administration and make it easier for the state to secure federal help. He said Ohio's elected Republican officials frequently call him seeking money for the state, adding that he would be less inclined to accommodate Democrats if they win key races. Referring to Acton, Trump said: "But I'm not going to help her." Husted is counting on Trump to motivate supporters who might otherwise skip the midterms, but the senator also directly criticized Brown, a veteran Democrat, as someone who has accomplished little in his political career. "He's been in office for 50 years — can you name one thing that he has done for you?" Husted said at the rally. A spokesperson for Brown's campaign criticized Husted for backing Trump's policy on Iran and said Husted supported "sweetheart tax deals" that lured data centers to Ohio. "Jon Husted puts corporations and billionaires first every time, and we all pay for it," Brown spokesperson Lauren Chou said in an email to Reuters. Trump garnered more than 55% of the Ohio vote in the 2024 presidential election, but economic concerns since then have sunk his approval ratings. Ohio gasoline prices increased 35% over the past year to $4.16 per gallon on average, according to AAA, which compiles data on automobile travel. Trump's trade policy with Canada has led to retaliatory Canadian tariffs that affect about $3 billion worth of Ohio exports, based on 2025 figures, according to a CBC report. DEBATE ON DATA CENTERS Talking to reporters shortly before addressing Saturday's rally, Husted said the US has to win the Iran war "on our terms" and in the interim, he is "showing people that I'm fighting for lower prices." He spoke to a sympathetic crowd at the rally, but he also needs to sell his message to people like independent voter Jonathan Smith. Smith, a 19-year-old construction worker, held a sign reading, "Where are my lower gas prices?" outside his former high school in Vandalia, north of Dayton. "I've got a wedding to save up for, and with gas prices continuously going up, it's getting harder and harder to put aside money," said Smith, adding he is still deciding whom to vote for in the Senate race. Outside political groups have poured [USN:L6N458188 TEXT:"tens of millions"] of dollars into Ohio, making Husted-Brown the second-most-expensive Senate race in the country, according to Federal Election Commission filings. Rallygoers shared mixed opinions on the hot-button issue of data centers in the state. "I'm not huge on the AI data centers," Samuel Clevenger, 20, said when discussing Husted's candidacy. But the apprentice plumber said he was encouraged to vote by Trump's attention to the state, as well as his 2025 policy capping taxes on overtime. On the other side of the rally venue, Brenda White, 60, held a sign encouraging building in her northeastern Ohio town: "DATA CENTER SOUTH LORAIN." As Husted met voters in the bleachers, she urged the senator to support the center's construction in place of a steel mill. "You want a data center there?" Husted asked. Before White posed for her photo with Husted, a man in the senator's entourage asked: "Can we do it without the sign?"

item.title: New term gives US Supreme Court's Thomas and Alito more chances to wield power
item.description: The two oldest and most conservative justices are at the height of their influence.
item.dc:creator: Jan Wolfe
item.content:encoded: The new US Supreme Court term that begins on Monday presents opportunities for its two eldest and most conservative justices, Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito, to help push US law further rightward on contentious issues such as gun rights, religion in public schools and voting restrictions. Thomas, 78, has served on the top US judicial body since 1991, making him the [USN:L1N41E02Q TEXT:"second-longest-serving justice"] in American history. Alito, 76, has served since 2006. Earlier in their tenures, they often found themselves in dissent in major decisions, but the court, with a 6-3 conservative majority since 2020, has shifted dramatically to the right. Thomas and Alito now are perhaps at the height of their influence and have been lavished with praise by Republican President Donald Trump . 'WHY LEAVE?' If either were to retire, that would clear the way for Trump to nominate a younger conservative replacement who could serve for decades in the lifetime position. But, at least for now, according to legal experts, they appear more interested in wielding that power than stepping aside. "They have been waiting for a long time to be in the position," political science professor Kevin McMahon of Trinity College in Connecticut said of Thomas and Alito. "So why leave?" During the court's term that ended in June, Thomas and Alito helped deliver long-sought victories to the conservative legal movement. These included a [USN:S0N3YR013 TEXT:"ruling"] expanding presidential control over regulatory agencies, and a [USN:S0N3YR00L TEXT:"decision"] further limiting the scope of the Voting Rights Act, the landmark 1965 law intended to eliminate racial discrimination in voting. Thomas and Alito have been Trump's most reliable votes in cases involving his extraordinary exertion of presidential powers. [USN:L1N45H0WL TEXT:"More such cases are coming"] during the new nine-month term, including two involving Trump's hardline [USN:S0N43101E TEXT:"immigration policies"]. The court's docket also includes November 3 arguments in a [USN:L1N4130K0 TEXT:"challenge"] to a Colorado law requiring preschools receiving taxpayer money to enroll children of same-sex couples, the latest clash between religious rights and LGBT protections to reach the justices. The justices also may take up a case examining whether a Texas law that requires public elementary and high schools to display the [USN:L1N45G0IM TEXT:"biblical Ten Commandments"] in classrooms comports with the US Constitution's prohibition on the government establishing or endorsing any particular religion or promoting religion over nonreligion. On December 2, the court will [USN:S0N3YR01V TEXT:"hear"] arguments over whether states can ban AR-15s and other semiautomatic rifles, an opportunity for the conservative justices to further expand gun rights. Thomas and Alito have been instrumental in major guns rulings since 2008. On December 8, the court will [USN:S0N41Y01G TEXT:"consider"] whether Arizona can mandate that people registering to vote provide proof of citizenship, a Republican-backed measure critics have called an effort to make it harder for groups who tend to support Democratic candidates to register. Legal experts said these cases give Thomas and Alito chances to build on some of their most influential earlier rulings and target more Supreme Court precedents they consider misguided. "They have more they want to accomplish, and I expect them to keep pushing on a host of issues," McMahon said, adding that they even may envision themselves serving as a check on a potential future Democratic president beginning in 2029. "They're still in their seventies," McMahon said. "And for a Supreme Court justice, it's not unprecedented that you stay on the bench well into your eighties." 'LEGENDS, BOTH' Thomas and Alito backed every major Trump administration policy that came before the court last term, unlike the three conservative justices Trump appointed during his first term — Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett. Those three all have compiled very conservative records as justices but in a few major cases sided against Trump. Trump [USN:L6N45N0QS TEXT:"told"] Time magazine this week he regretted nominating all three, calling them disloyal. "I gave them the position of a lifetime, and they vote against me often," Trump said. Thomas and Alito, on the other hand, are "[USN:FWN4570D3 TEXT:"legends, both"]," Trump said last month after they dissented from a decision that blocked his plans to restrict mail-in voting. "Alito and Thomas are the two who have figured out how to never get into Trump's doghouse," University of Minnesota political science professor Timothy Johnson said. Alito rejected the notion that he is a rubber stamp for Trump and his administration, telling the Wall Street Journal in August: "I vote in every case the way I think the case should be decided. If that means a high correlation with what Trump wants, fine. If it means zero correlation with what Trump wants, fine as well." 'A VALUABLE CONTRIBUTION' Speculation among court watchers about a possible vacancy has ramped up as the two men draw closer to the average age of retirement for Supreme Court justices since 2000 — about 80 years old — and with the November 3 US congressional elections looming. If Democrats take control of the Senate, they could try to block Trump's nominee to fill any vacancy created by the retirement or death of a sitting justice. Alito tamped down retirement speculation for now, telling the Wall Street Journal: "Obviously, I'm here for another term." The term runs through the end of June. In a CBS News interview excerpt released on Friday, Alito said he thought about retiring this year, calling retirement something someone his age must think about every year. "But I thought that I could still make a valuable contribution, which is why I became a justice and a judge in the first place," Alito said. "It's too hard to predict, for anybody, particularly when you reach a certain age, what your situation will be a year from now, two years from now, and so forth," Alito said. "And it's too hard to predict what the political situation will be, and what any president might do with respect to a replacement." ABORTION RIGHTS Alito has a lot of influence in conversations among the court's conservatives, said Peter Canellos, author of a recent Alito biography titled "Revenge for the Sixties." "A lot of the action on the Supreme Court right now is conservative on conservative," Canellos said. "It's entirely a discussion among conservatives." Canellos said Alito's influence was highlighted by Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization, perhaps the most important ruling he has authored. It overturned the 1973 Roe v. Wade precedent that had recognized a woman's constitutional right to have an abortion. Chief Justice John Roberts, a stalwart conservative, dissented from the portion of Alito's ruling that reversed Roe. "I think over the years Alito has thought of himself as an instrumental justice," Canellos said. "You can see in many cases, Dobbs included, that his key ability is to bring the three Trump appointees to his side, rather than Chief Justice Roberts' side, when the two of them disagree." In Dobbs, Gorsuch, Kavanaugh and Barrett joined Alito. "I suspect that Alito felt that even if he were replaced by a true conservative, which was the core of the argument why he should resign, it was not in any way preordained that that person would have the kind of influence that he has," Canellos added. Alito has long criticized a 1990 Supreme Court precedent that limits the ability of people to seek religious exemptions from generally applicable laws. Religious rights advocates have said that ruling infringes on First Amendment protections for free exercise of religion. The 1990 ruling specifically held that the First Amendment does not protect people who participate in illegal acts — in that case, the use of an illegal hallucinogenic drug — as part of a religious ceremony. The religious freedom case being argued in November, called St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy, gives Alito and the other conservative justices a chance to cast doubt on the 1990 precedent, known as Employment Division v. Smith. 'WHY NOT CONTINUE?' The case involving state-level bans on assault-style rifles may give Thomas a chance to clarify a test he laid out in one of his most impactful rulings, a 2022 case called New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen. Under this test, gun control measures must be "consistent with this nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation" — not simply advance an important government interest — in order to comply with the Second Amendment right to keep and bear arms. Some judges have said this wording does not provide clear guidance, producing inconsistent results. "He has clearly expressed frustration that his colleagues have dodged reviews of assault-weapon prohibitions, making these consolidated challenges from Connecticut and Illinois a long-sought vehicle to establish a nationwide constitutional rule that includes these specific guns," Johnson said of Thomas. Thomas has not addressed retirement rumors, but in the past has hinted at a lengthy tenure. McMahon said Thomas may want to become the longest-serving justice, a milestone he would reach in May 2028. "If you're that close, and you have the setup that he has, why not continue?" McMahon asked.

item.title: Latvia PM Kulbergs wins election held under shadow of Ukraine war
item.description: Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs' centrist, pro-Ukraine United List party won Saturday's parliamentary election by an unexpectedly wide margin, partial results showed, with many voters on edge amid warnings of potential Russian aggression.
item.dc:creator: Andrius Sytas, Terje Solsvik
item.content:encoded: Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs' centrist, pro-Ukraine United List party won Saturday's parliamentary election by an unexpectedly wide margin, partial results showed, with many voters on edge amid warnings of potential Russian aggression. With 88% of ballots counted, United List was on 36.6%, followed by the populist, MAGA-style Latvia First on 13.4%. Latvia First had courted the country's substantial ethnic Russian minority in the run-up to the vote. Baltic countries have warned for months that Russia is mounting sabotage, cyber and other hybrid attacks across Europe to erode support for Ukraine and sow fear, although Western officials dismiss concerns that Moscow is capable of launching a direct assault on NATO, of which Latvia is a member. Russia says such accusations are baseless and the result of anti-Russian hysteria. Reacting to exit poll readings earlier in the evening, Kulbergs said he hoped to remain prime minister but that he would not want to govern with Latvia First. According to partial results, he will still need coalition allies to form a government. "It's remarkably good. I was not expecting such a result," Kulbergs said at his party's headquarters in Riga. Third in the exit poll ranking was the pro-Russian Sovereign Power party, on 11.6%, followed by the nationalist National Alliance, which promotes a hardline approach to the Kremlin, at 9.1%. SHADOW OF UKRAINE WAR A businessman and amateur rally driver, Kulbergs, 47, came to power in May after the previous coalition crumbled over its handling of incidents in which [USN:L1N41K03T TEXT:"stray military drones flew"] undetected into Latvia. Though the drones were Ukrainian, officials [USN:L8N41X1AC TEXT:"have blamed Russia"] for causing them to divert from their flight paths. "The priority, in my view, is, of course, security – security in Latvia," said Megija Nordena, 21, from Riga. "And then ... as a student, I’d say support for students, the economy, and also support for pensioners." Throughout his campaign, Kulbergs has also promised more anti-drone capabilities for Latvia and to maintain defence spending at 5% of gross domestic product, one of the highest levels in NATO. His pro-Kremlin rivals said Latvia should stop any aid to Ukraine and should instead focus more on cost-of-living issues, particularly among the country's Russian-speaking minority. "Our voters want peace, to stop looking for shelters, to no longer experience the air alerts," Sovereign Power party leader Julia Stepanenko told Reuters. "The war must not be encouraged in any way, including by financing it ... Ukraine must win, but through peace talks." The ethnic Russian minority in Latvia is split between those who feel embarrassed or angry about the Kremlin's war in Ukraine, and those frustrated with policies at home aimed at limiting their influence on public life that many see as discriminatory. Latvia, with a population of 1.9 million, is sandwiched between the Baltic Sea, and Russia and Belarus to the east, with EU and NATO allies Estonia and Lithuania to the north and south.

item.title: At Cornell, rape allegations spark outrage, soul-searching over campus culture
item.description: Students have scheduled a rally for Monday to call for more measures to protect victims.
item.dc:creator: Maria Tsvetkova
item.content:encoded: Cornell University student Sophia Riley Sim skipped classes this week, consumed by allegations in a lawsuit that several members of a fraternity raped a young woman in 2024 and troubled by how her university handled the case. "Cornell has failed our community through its lack of accountability, transparency, and failure to address the state of the Cornell student body at this time," Sim, a junior, said at a public hearing on sexual assault organized by Cornell's Student Assembly on Thursday. "There has been a lack of meaningful communication from university leadership, administrators, and faculty." The Ivy League school has defended its handling of the matter, saying it launched a comprehensive investigation and barred the Chi Phi fraternity involved in the alleged assault from campus. The school said it imposed a range of disciplinary measures, including expulsions. It did not immediately respond to a request for additional comment. The hearing, held in one of Cornell's historic halls, came days after the allegations became public with the [USN:L1N45N0UA TEXT:"filing of a civil lawsuit"] and the announcement that a criminal investigation would be reopened. The case has reignited scrutiny of how law enforcement and universities handle sexual assault complaints, with students questioning whether processes are enough to protect them. It has also drawn the attention of New York state officials, who have appointed a special prosecutor to investigate. FEELING UNSAFE At the Assembly hearing, speakers recounted experiences with sexual assault, broke down in tears and criticized the response of the prestigious university. The Student Assembly - which represents Cornell's undergraduate students and can make proposals to the university's bodies or officers - unanimously approved a resolution calling on Cornell administrators to provide a full account of how the investigation was handled. It also asked the university to disclose any disciplinary measures imposed on the accused students, and publish annual reports on the outcomes of any future sexual misconduct cases. Organizers asked that many of the dozens of speakers at the hearing not be identified or recorded. One student said she had worked all her life to be accepted to Cornell and now felt that it had not been worth it. Several others said they did not feel safe on the 2,300-acre campus in New York's Finger Lakes region. Thirty-five percent of undergraduate women reported experiencing nonconsensual sexual contact involving force or incapacitation since entering Cornell, according to a university survey conducted in 2025 and published on its website. That figure was up from 20% in 2021. "WE ARE GOING TO FIGHT" The lawsuit alleges fraternity members supplied the woman with alcohol, marijuana and ketamine before sexually assaulting her after she became incapacitated. It also alleges Cornell failed to adequately punish some of the accused students and allowed some to seek reduced penalties by writing essays. Cornell denied that essays were the only punishment meted out. The New York Times, citing internal Cornell documents, said the men all denied any wrongdoing, with some saying the sex was consensual and others denying participation. Cornell students have scheduled a rally for Monday to call for additional measures to protect victims. Jane Wang, a public policy major, said she had reported a sexual assault to the university and that the process caused additional distress. "In the midst of all of my mental, physical, and emotional recovery from the assault, I was also met with an abundance of paperwork, very little instruction on how to navigate it, and no follow up from our office about an outcome," she said. The Ivy League school said in a statement on its website that it could not provide full information regarding individual students and disciplinary outcomes because of restrictions imposed by privacy laws. "Our adherence to privacy laws should not be interpreted as indifference to the seriousness of the conduct at issue," the statement said. A handful of other female students told the hearing they had been sexually assaulted on Cornell's campus in the past, without sharing details. Saanya Agarwal, Cornell University's student women's issues representative, said the findings of the 2025 survey on sexual assaults were unacceptable. "Clearly, this is an issue our campus and campuses throughout the United States... it's something that we're not going to accept," said Agarwal. "We are going to fight."

item.title: Minutes from disaster: Inside the flydubai flight as it plunged from the sky
item.description: In just a few minutes, the plane lurched into violent climbs and dives, shed some 17,000 feet of altitude, and surged to nearly 600 knots of ground speed, about 45% faster than its normal cruising pace.
item.dc:creator: Vijdan Kawoosa, Adrián Blanco
item.content:encoded: Passengers and crew on a flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv on September 30 foiled what Israeli officials said was an attempt by the co-pilot to crash the aircraft, averting disaster. A reserve crew then took control and landed the plane in Saudi Arabia. Click here to read more. Flydubai flight 1073, carrying 174 passengers and crew members, departed Dubai for Tel Aviv at 7:05 a.m. local time (0305 GMT), and was cruising at 34,000 feet over Saudi Arabia. Limited three-dimensional tracking data from Flightradar24 shows the aircraft turned right and fell more than 16,000 feet in just over 30 seconds. The aircraft pulled up and recovered some altitude before dropping again. While the exact sequence of events remains unclear, the co-pilot stabbed the captain in what Israeli officials said was an apparent attempt to crash the plane. About eight minutes after the first plunge, the plane transmitted squawk 7700, the code for a general emergency. About six minutes after that, the squawk changed to 7500, the code for unlawful interference. The aircraft entered Jordanian airspace and then turned back toward Saudi Arabia. More than an hour later, the flight landed safely at Tabuk airport in Saudi Arabia. More detailed two dimensional flight data shows the aircraft’s movements were even more erratic. In just a few minutes, the plane that had been cruising smoothly at 34,000 feet lurched into violent climbs and dives, shed some 17,000 feet of altitude, and surged to nearly 600 knots of ground speed, about 45% faster than its normal cruising pace, before slowly steadying itself. Although the Flydubai 1073 aircraft recovered from the plunge, its initial descent was strikingly steep. The trajectory can be compared with the rapid descents of aircraft involved in several major crashes, a Reuters analysis showed. At its steepest point, the plane was losing altitude at about 544 feet (166 metres) per second, roughly equivalent to the height of 44 storeys of the Empire State Building every second. The wounded captain managed to unlock the cockpit door, allowing passengers to subdue the attacker, Israeli officials said. A reserve crew that had been aboard landed the plane at Tabuk airport in Saudi Arabia. Flydubai said on Wednesday the circumstances surrounding the incident are still being investigated. Reuters was not able to contact the co-pilot, who has been detained.

item.title: Wall St Week Ahead Spiking bond yields, midterms, earnings to test US stocks' typical fourth-quarter strength
item.description: Bond yields, the midterms and earnings likely will test US stocks' typical fourth-quarter strength.
item.dc:creator: Lewis Krauskopf
item.content:encoded: Investors head into a part of the calendar that tends to be upbeat for US stocks, but that seasonal strength is under threat from a number of challenges, including a surge in bond yields and the market's apparent dependence on massive AI spending. As the fourth quarter kicks off, the stock market is already on pace for a solid year. The benchmark S&P 500 (.SPX) as of Friday had gained nearly 13% in 2026, and sat about 1% below its mid-August record high. Markets face a busy end of 2026, with the start of corporate earnings season and a pivotal Federal Reserve meeting in coming weeks, along with the looming November 3 midterm elections that will decide control of the US Congress. "It does tend to be a seasonally strong period, however I think this year investors are facing some headwinds as we go into the fourth quarter," said Tracie McMillion, head of global asset allocation strategy at the Wells Fargo Investment Institute. Q4 TENDS TO SEE STOCK GAINS Since 1945, the S&P 500 averaged an increase of 4.2% in the fourth quarter, with the index posting gains 85% of the time, according to research firm CFRA. That average percentage rise is more than twice that of the other three quarters. Fourth quarters of midterm years have generally been even stronger, with an average gain of 6.4%, as stocks "benefit from the lifting of election uncertainty," Sam Stovall, chief investment strategist at CFRA, said in a note. While fourth quarters tend to shine, mid-term years overall historically have been subpar, a trend stocks have defied so far in 2026. The S&P 500 has averaged a 15% dip in midterm years historically, while the deepest drop so far this year has only been 9%, according to McMillion of the Wells Fargo institute. The firm is on "high alert" for a pullback between now and election day, she said, for example, if it looks like the Democrats can wrest full control of Congress from President Donald Trump's Republican party. "If we were to see a change in the leadership in the House and the Senate combined, then we think that that could have some policy ramifications that could impact the markets," she said, while adding that a pullback could be a buying opportunity. SPIKING YIELDS IN FOCUS, FED MINUTES DUE The most immediate issue for stock investors is the jump in bond yields. The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield on Thursday hit 5.34%, its [USN:L6N45N12O TEXT:"highest level in 24 years"]. Yields, which rise when bond prices fall, have soared amid expectations for strong economic growth, surging energy costs that are driving up inflation, and increased competition for capital as companies issue debt to fund AI expansions. Higher yields likely already are impeding the market's advance, investors said. They can create more investment competition for equities and pressure stock valuations, while translating into more expensive borrowing costs throughout the economy. "The interest rate story is the biggest headwind," said Chuck Carlson, chief executive officer at Horizon Investment Services. "You're going to need some relief on that front. I don't necessarily think the market will tank per se, but to get a meaningful rally in the face of that, I think is going to be a struggle for the market." Another factor driving yields is the Fed's plans for monetary policy. The US central bank hiked interest rates last month for the first time in three years in an effort to cool above-target inflation. Minutes covering that meeting will be released on Wednesday and could offer Wall Street clues about the Fed's rate outlook, including the potential for another hike in October or December. Following [USN:L1N45N170 TEXT:"weaker-than-expected jobs data"] on Friday, markets kept bets that the Fed would likely hold off on a second straight hike at its meeting later in the month. BIG EARNINGS GROWTH SEEN, AI SPEND IN SPOTLIGHT PepsiCo (PEP.O) and Delta Air Lines (DAL.N) are among the handful of large companies set to post third-quarter results next week, before major banks kick off the reporting season more broadly the following week. This year, corporate profits have surpassed already-lofty projections, propelling the stock market's rally. But they have also raised the bar for stellar performance that could test the market. S&P 500 companies overall are expected to have increased earnings by more than 30% in the third quarter from a year earlier, according to LSEG IBES data. Particularly important are developments related to the massive spending by AI hyperscalers to build out infrastructure, which has lifted profits at a wealth of companies. The US stock market's performance has been highly correlated to the AI theme, said Nelson Yu, head of equities at AllianceBernstein. As it relates to AI this upcoming earnings season, "the number one thing to watch for is capex revisions from the hyperscalers," Yu said. "Because that does kind of start the whole chain."

item.title: Who are the Houthis, Iran’s allies in Yemen?
item.description: Yemen's Saudi-backed government announced the start of a military counteroffensive against the Iran-backed Houthis, aimed at seizing the territory under their control.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Yemen's Saudi-backed government announced the start of a [USN:L1N45Q02D TEXT:"military counteroffensive"] against the Iran-backed Houthis, aimed at seizing the territory under their control. Renewed warfare between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia has reignited Yemen's frozen civil war and heightened risks to Red Sea shipping, further disrupting Middle Eastern energy exports already choked by Iran in the Strait of Hormuz. WHO ARE THE HOUTHIS? The Houthis are a military, political and religious movement that rules over most of northwest Yemen and has [USN:L6N43M0M9 TEXT:"disrupted global trade and energy"] markets with attacks on cargo ships and tankers in the Red Sea. It began firing on ships in the Red Sea and launching drones and missiles at Israel in November 2023, saying it was doing so in support of Palestinians during Israel's war in Gaza that began the previous month. Those attacks on Red Sea shipping, as well as on Saudi Arabia, resumed this year in response to the United States' war on the Houthis' close ally Iran. WHAT DO THE HOUTHIS WANT? The group emerged in far north Yemen in the 1990s as a revival movement for the Zaydi sect of Shi'ite Islam, which had once ruled Yemen but whose northern heartland had become impoverished and marginalised. It fought a series of guerrilla wars against Yemen's national army and a brief border conflict with Sunni Saudi Arabia. When Yemen's longtime president Ali Abdullah Saleh was brought down in the 2011 "Arab spring" protests, the group consolidated its control over northern Yemen, rejecting a Gulf-backed political transition. With Iranian support, the group's secretive leader, Abdul Malik al-Houthi, was meanwhile turning his faction of mountain fighters into a force of tens of thousands. In 2014 they seized the capital Sanaa, driving the internationally recognised government south towards Aden. WHAT'S BEHIND THE HOUTHI CONFLICT WITH SAUDI ARABIA? Fearful of growing Iranian influence in Yemen and chaos on its borders, Saudi Arabia led a military intervention against the Houthis in early 2015 to dislodge the group, restore the government and revive the transition plan. The resulting [USN:L6N3Y307N TEXT:"civil war"] triggered one of the world's biggest humanitarian crises and led to years of bitter fighting and devastating airstrikes by Saudi Arabia and its coalition partners, including the United Arab Emirates. However, neither side was able to gain much ground in Yemen's mountainous terrain, and the Houthis remained in control over the northwest, where most of the population lives. They demonstrated significant missile and drone capabilities, attacking oil installations and vital infrastructure in Saudi Arabia and the UAE. After years of fighting, the UN brokered a 2022 truce between the warring sides in Yemen that maintained peace until this year. HOW MUCH DAMAGE CAN THE HOUTHIS DO WITH ATTACKS IN THE RED SEA AND SAUDI ARABIA? The group's attacks on Red Sea shipping between 2023 and 2025 significantly disrupted global trade, forcing cargo ships travelling between Europe and Asia to take a long, expensive route around Africa. Their threats to oil tankers during the Iran war have added to the squeeze on energy out of the Gulf after Tehran mostly choked off the Strait of Hormuz, adding to a global oil crisis. Some Houthi missile and drone attacks have caused significant damage in Saudi Arabia and the UAE over the years, but have proven less effective against targets further north, such as Israel. LINKS WITH IRAN Iran champions the Houthis as part of its regional "Axis of Resistance", which also includes Lebanon's Hezbollah and Iraqi Shi'ite militias, though its ties with the Yemeni movement are less clear than with those other groups. The Houthis do not recognise Iran's supreme leader as their ultimate religious authority in the same way Hezbollah and the Iraqi groups do. Their motivations are also mainly domestic, though they are ideologically aligned with Iran. The US says Iran has armed, funded and trained the Houthis with help from Hezbollah. The Houthis deny being an Iranian proxy and say they develop their own weapons.

item.title: OFRMO Summary
item.description: Le président yéménite annonce une offensive d'envergure contre les Houthis
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Le président yéménite annonce une offensive d'envergure contre les Houthis 4 octobre (Reuters) - Le président yéménite, dont le gouvernement est soutenu par l'Arabie saoudite, a annoncé dimanche le lancement d'une vaste opération militaire contre les rebelles houthis pro-iraniens, visant à reprendre le contrôle des territoires qu'ils occupent. Des explosions entendues pendant la visite du chancelier allemand à Kyiv KYIV, 4 octobre (Reuters) - Des sirènes d'alerte aérienne et des explosions ont retenti dimanche dans la capitale ukrainienne, Kyiv, alors que le chancelier allemand Friedrich Merz rendait visite au président ukrainien Volodimir Zelensky dans le cadre du renouvellement du soutien de l'Allemagne à l'Ukraine. Éthiopie-La capitale du Tigré sous contrôle des forces gouvernementales-sources 4 octobre (Reuters) - Les forces gouvernementales éthiopiennes et les milices alliées ont repris le contrôle de la capitale du Tigré, ont rapporté à Reuters trois sources dimanche, infligeant ainsi un revers majeur à l'alliance d'opposition qui gouverne cette région du nord. Les Brésiliens se rendent aux urnes dans un contexte de forte polarisation BRASILIA/SÃO PAULO, 4 octobre (Reuters) - Les Brésiliens se rendront aux urnes dimanche pour le premier tour d'une élection annoncée très serrée, après une campagne marquée par des scandales de corruption, des inquiétudes économiques et des accusations d'ingérence américaine. Espagne-Deux morts dans des inondations en Catalogne 4 octobre (Reuters) - Deux personnes ont péri et une autre est portée disparue à la suite de fortes pluies et d'inondations dans la région de Catalogne, en Espagne, ont rapporté dimanche les autorités. Le Premier ministre letton en passe de diriger une coalition pro-ukrainienne RIGA, 4 octobre (Reuters) - Le Premier ministre letton, Andris Kulbergs, devrait conserver le pouvoir, sa "Liste unie", formation centriste et pro-ukrainienne, étant en passe de signer une large victoire, la plus importante aux élections législatives depuis que la Lettonie a retrouvé son indépendance en 1991. L'Ukraine va intensifier ses frappes sur les raffineries russes KYIV, 3 octobre (Reuters) - L'Ukraine va intensifier ses attaques contre les raffineries russes en réponse à la nouvelle stratégie de frappes aériennes menée par Moscou visant à forcer la population à quitter Kyiv et d'autres villes, sans pour autant prendre pour cible les civils, a déclaré le président ukrainien Volodimir Zelensky. La Russie continuera à pilonner Kyiv, invite les diplomates à quitter la capitale ukrainienne 3 octobre (Reuters) - La Russie a déclaré samedi qu'elle continuerait à mener des frappes sur Kyiv et d'autres villes ukrainiennes, exhortant les ressortissants étrangers et les diplomates à quitter la capitale ukrainienne. USA/MIDTERMS-Trump tente de mobiliser les électeurs dans l'Ohio VANDALIA, Ohio, 3 octobre (Reuters) - Le président américain Donald Trump a adopté un ton combatif lors d'un rassemblement organisé samedi dans l'Ohio, l'un des Etats où le scrutin pour remporter un siège au Sénat lors des élections de mi-mandat pourrait être décisif. Le copilote de Flydubai a tenté de commettre un "attentat" avec une hache - procureur Le copilote du vol FZ1073 de Flydubai, à destination d'Israël, a tenté de commettre un "attentat terroriste" pendant le vol avec une hache se trouvant dans le cockpit, a déclaré samedi le procureur général des Emirats arabes unis.
